sweep_summary: Seven title hits for English; none changes the catalog's weight-hedged coding from Hayes 1982. Peck 1971 (Kivung 4(3)) was located in the LLM/Kivung open archive, downloaded (pp. 194-207; pp. 192-193 missing from the scan) and scanned: it is a review of Vanderslice's rules for assigning sentence accent and intonation to text and presupposes dictionary-listed word stress, so it is silent on placement. Peperkamp 1997 (dissertation, print only) and 1996 (Kleinhenz volume, paywalled; Glottolog's '1966'/'Acta Linguistica Hafniensia' are errors) are about prosodic words and clitics in Romance/Dutch, judged from the author's open GLOT 1999 summary and abstracts. Aitken 1984 and Petyt 1985 use 'accent' in the regional-pronunciation sense (not relevant). Pike 1945 (intonation-marking procedure in Fries's ESL manual) is on archive.org only as restricted lending; Hayes 1995 (already listed) has no open copy and would only restate Hayes 1982. No new authoritative stress statement found; nothing to acquire at high priority.

Nida adds no placement rule but documents the rhythmic retraction of final-accented attributives before initially-stressed heads (the later 'Rhythm Rule') and the atonic status of determiners, which is compatible with any characterisation of English as having non-fixed, lexically variable word stress. Note that the open link recorded by Glottolog (sil.org/acpub/repository/) is dead; the SIL archives page for 11827 also 404s; the Florida scan on archive.org (synopsisofenglis00nida) is not access-restricted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for the placement of word stress is given (the book is a syntax; the 1960 preface says intonation 'is here treated only under Bloomfield's taxeme of modulation'). What it does record is rhythmic stress retraction: polysyllabic attributives that carry final accent in isolation or after the verb (Chinese, fourteen, dead-drunk, unknown, well-made..) take initial stress when they immediately precede a head noun with initial stress ('a 'Chinese 'bank' vs 'a Chin'ese in'vasion', 'the 'fourteen 'boys' vs 'He was four'teen'); before heads with an initial unstressed syllable the choice varies. It also notes that determiners (my, our, the, a..) are usually atonic except under emphatic or contrastive stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the compound/phrase examples are marked with primary accents only ('a 'Chinese 'bank / a Chin'ese in'vasion').
new_statements.exceptions: Variation before heads whose first syllable is unstressed; the pattern is stated for 'the writer's speech' (American English, 1943 dissertation).

new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement of where the main stress falls. The grammar assumes a 'main stress' (also 'chief stress', 'full stress') and a 'secondary stress' per word and uses them as conditioning environments: the vowel [ɔ] (mid-back-wide-round) occurs only in syllables without the main stress; 'the stress h' exists but is absent where original stress has been lost; unrounding of ME. u in 'could', 'should' and the voicing of OE. þ to ð are attributed to secondary stress; several sources of n occur 'only with secondary, or absence of stress'; hw becomes w in unstressed positions. Pronouns have stressed, secondary and unstressed forms.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No general word-stress rule is stated anywhere in the grammar. The chapters are organised by vowels in accented vs unaccented syllables (Chs. II-III vs Ch. V, §§ 241-249: vowels in unaccented syllables weaken to ə, i or are lost; § 242 lists prefixed words such as befuə(r) 'before', begin, əbat 'about' as having the principal accent on the syllable after the prefix; § 249 gives weak forms of function words governed by the sentence accent). Placement is stated only for particular classes: diphthongs and triphthongs are stressed on their first element (p. 3); the reflexive pronouns mi-sen/-sel/-seln, ði-sen, i-sen, wə-sen etc. carry the stress on the second syllable (§ 353); adverbs of manner in -li are stem-stressed except siuəlĭ 'surely' and əkuədinlái 'accordingly', which stress the suffix (§ 399). In the dialect specimens a raised dot marks a strong stress only where it is not obvious (p. 212).
new_statements.exceptions: Suffix stress in siuəlĭ 'surely' and əkuədinlái 'accordingly' (§ 399, p. 166); § 242 (p. 68) lists edikeet 'educate', kontreeri 'contrary', redzeste(r) 'register', spekteklz 'spectacles' (scanned spellings) as words whose initial syllable is not weakened.
new_statements.identity_note: Wright 1892 describes the Windhill dialect (West Riding of Yorkshire, near Bradford), not Standard English. Fon 2002 and Herman 1998 analyse English spoken by subjects recorded at Ohio State University; the variety is not specified in the pages read. Walrod 2006 is about Philippine languages (Ga'dang, Ilocano, Bontoc, Ifugao, Ibaloi, Tagalog) and is attached to English only by content language. The three SIL book reviews and Dooley 2007 concern English in general (vocabulary, prepositions, word history, discourse topicality).
